what_its_for: Tiagabine is used along with other medicines to help control partial seizures (a type of epilepsy) in adults and children 12 years and older. It works by calming overactive electrical signals in the brain that cause seizures.
how_to_take: Take tiagabine exactly as your doctor tells you. Always take it WITH food — this helps the medicine work more steadily and reduces side effects like dizziness. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Do not crush or chew the tablets. Take it at the same times each day to keep a steady level in your body.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a low dose and slowly increase it over several weeks until your seizures are well controlled. A typical starting dose for adults is 4 mg once daily. Your doctor may increase this by 4 to 8 mg each week. Most adults take between 32 to 56 mg per day, divided into 2 to 4 doses throughout the day. Never change your dose on your own — always follow your doctor's instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is not too close to your next scheduled dose. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you miss several doses in a row, call your doctor before restarting, as stopping suddenly can trigger more seizures.
storage: Store tiagabine at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use medicine that is expired — check the date on the bottle and dispose of old medicine safely.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking tiagabine — it can increase dizziness, confusion, and the risk of seizures. Do not drive, operate heavy machinery, or do activities that require alertness until you know how this medicine affects you, because it can cause dizziness and drowsiness. Avoid suddenly stopping this medication without talking to your doctor first, as this can cause withdrawal seizures. Tell your doctor about all other medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements you take, as many drugs can interact with tiagabine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: new or worsening seizures, confusion or difficulty thinking clearly, weakness on one side of your body, sudden vision changes, signs of a serious skin reaction (rash, blisters, peeling skin), thoughts of hurting yourself or depression, or unusual behavior changes. Contact your doctor if you have ongoing dizziness, severe stomach upset, tremors (shaking), or difficulty with coordination. Seek emergency help immediately if you have a seizure that does not stop.
when_it_works: Tiagabine does not work right away. It may take several weeks before you notice fewer or less severe seizures, because your doctor will be slowly increasing your dose to find the right level for you. Even if you feel well and your seizures seem controlled, keep taking your medicine every day as directed. Do not stop taking it on your own.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Seizure medicines can pose risks to an unborn baby, but stopping medicine can also be dangerous. Your doctor will help weigh the risks and benefits. Breastfeeding: It is not known if tiagabine passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: Tiagabine is approved for children 12 years and older. It is not recommended for younger children. Older adults: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects like dizziness and falls, so use extra caution. Liver disease: If you have liver problems, your doctor may need to adjust your dose, as tiagabine is processed by the liver.
